title: Water infrastructure rates and 2024 budget timeline
subtitle: Shortened budget amendment period, closed session on two land matters, and a councillor's declared interest.
overview: Council held a special meeting focused on the Water Infrastructure Program (WIP) for 2024 to 2027. Staff presented three rate options, ranging from 6.3% to 8.6% a year, which would add about $77 to $105 annually to the average homeowner's utility bill. Staff recommended the lowest option, 6.3% a year for four years. Many councillors spoke in support. No motion was made on this item, and the rate will come back through the 2024 budget process.

Council also approved the 2024 budget timelines and shortened the 30-day period for amending the Mayor's proposed budget so it ends with the meeting on December 14, 2023 {{vote:m1}}. That sets when residents and councillors will see the budget finalized.

Council went into a closed session on two land acquisition and disposition matters {{vote:m2}}. The minutes report no outcome from it. One councillor declared a pecuniary interest in one of the matters and did not take part. For residents, the water rate increase would appear on utility bills starting in 2024, if approved in the budget.

decisions.detail: Council approved the 2024 budget timelines in report FIN-2023-417 and shortened the 30-day amendment period so it ends with the December 14, 2023 meeting.

debate: Staff said the 6.3% option meets legal requirements and funds maintenance and inspection programs, but cuts the original 2018 program targets by 33%. Inspections and trunk sewer and pumping station work were prioritized over road reconstruction.
Councillors cited a trunk sewer collapse that had little prior inspection and a repair cost of close to $6 million as the cost of deferring work. Several said delay would cost more later.

Councillors raised affordability for low-income residents and seniors. Staff pointed to a leak adjustment policy, a regional water audit program and a future water rate review, and mentioned a round-up donation idea used in another city.

Questions covered the Region of Waterloo's share of the increase. Staff said regional rates are projected but not guaranteed. One councillor asked for better coordination with the Region, and another worried that the lowest option could leave a gap for future councils.
Staff said construction costs are still rising faster than general inflation. They noted that the program allows for modest inflation and that it can do more road work if costs fall.
